note: đ (crossed d) is an English d. Plain d is a z sound in Hanoi.
d sounds like z in Hanoi (like y in the South).
x sounds like s.
nh is ny, as in canyon.
ph is f. ơ is the vowel you may have heard as "fuh".
gi sounds like z in Hanoi, just like d and r.
r is a z sound in Hanoi. au is a short ow, as in cow.
tr sounds like ch in Hanoi, the same as ch.
ng can start a word: say the ng of singer, then the vowel.
t has no puff of air: it sits between d and t. ay is short; compare tai (ear).
ai is a long ah-ee. tay (hand) is shorter, and the difference changes the word.
th is an English t with a puff of air, never the th of think. ư: say oo with spread lips.
kh is a soft throat sound, as in Scottish loch. ô is the o of go, held steady.
ă is a short ah, and it is always followed by a consonant.
â is a short uh, as in cup.
qu sounds like kw. ê is the e of hey, held steady.
ươ is a vowel pair said in one syllable: uu-uh.
Hanoi says -anh as aing: chanh is not like English chan.
Level tone: no mark, flat and in the middle of your voice.
Falling tone: start low and fall gently.
Rising tone. Same letters as ma (ghost) and mà (but).
Falling tone. Same letters as bán (to sell) and bạn (friend).
Rising tone: start in the middle and rise.
Heavy tone: low, short, with a catch in the throat.
Not only a tone pair: â has a vowel mark. bạn, with plain a, is a friend.
Level tone. múa, with the rising tone, is to dance.
Rising tone. mua, with no mark, is to buy.
Rising tone. cà, with the falling tone, is the first syllable of cà phê.
Falling tone. bỏ, with the dipping tone, means to throw away or to quit.
Rising tone. tôi, with no tone mark, means I.
Broken tone (the tilde). sửa, with the dipping tone, is to fix.
Dipping tone (the hook). sữa, with the broken tone, is milk.
Level tone. nằm, with the falling tone, is to lie down.
Falling tone. năm, with no tone mark, is five or a year.
Falling tone. ga, with no mark, is a train station.
Safe with anyone. People more often say Chào + a kinship word: Chào anh.

meaning: Hello. (to a woman a little older)
note: chị: a woman older than you, but not your parents' age.
Also spelled cám ơn. Add the person: Cảm ơn anh.
A little formal. Friends often say Chào + name, or Bye.

meaning: Hello. (to a man a little older)
note: anh: a man older than you, but not your parents' age.
em works for a younger man or a younger woman.
For someone about your own age. Never to an older person.

meaning: Hello. (politely, to a woman a little older)
note: The younger person says em for I, and ạ at the end adds respect.

meaning: How are you? (to a man a little older)
note: Keep không level: the word asks the question, not your voice.
No là before khỏe: it works like a verb.
To a woman a little older: Còn chị?

meaning: Thank you. (to a man a little older)
note: Naming the person sounds warmer than a bare Cảm ơn.
nhiều (a lot) goes at the end.
Literally: it's nothing.
The usual answer to Xin lỗi.

meaning: Nice to meet you. (to someone your age)
note: To a man a little older: Rất vui được gặp anh.
Often with the person at the end: Hẹn gặp lại chị.
Hanoi word. In the South: má.
Hanoi word. In the South: ba.
anh alone also means "you" to a man a little older than you.
em is any younger sibling; gái = female, trai = male.
ông and bà also mean "you" to an old man and an old woman.
chị alone also means "you" to a woman a little older than you.
Add trai or gái after em to say brother or sister.
Hanoi words. In the South: ba má.
Noun first, then the owner. With family, của is usually left out.
Not tôi chồng: the owner comes after the noun.
con = child; trai = male.
con gái can also mean a girl or a young woman.
nội = on your father's side.
ngoại = on your mother's side.

meaning: aunt (father's sister); you (to a woman your parents' age)
note: Also what you call a female teacher. You say cháu for I.

meaning: uncle (father's younger brother); you (to a man your parents' age)
note: You say cháu for I when you talk to chú.

meaning: grandchild; niece or nephew; I (to someone your parents' age or older)
note: Use cháu for I with cô, chú, ông and bà.
To introduce someone: Đây là + the person.
Falling tone. In twenty, thirty… it is mươi, with no mark: hai mươi.
After mươi, five is lăm, not năm.
Prices are counted in nghìn (thousands). The South says ngàn.
Level tone, and ai is a long ah-ee.
In the South, ba also means dad.
After mươi, four is often tư: hai mươi tư.
au is a short ow, as in cow.
Dipping tone (the hook). ay is short.
Rising tone. Eighteen is mười tám.
chín also means ripe or cooked.
After mười, five is lăm too.
After mươi, one is mốt (rising tone), not một.
tư is the usual four after mươi; hai mươi bốn is also heard.
The South says một ngàn.
Prices drop the word đồng in everyday speech.
con is the classifier for animals.
cái is the classifier for most objects.
quyển for books. The South says cuốn.
chiếc for vehicles and single items. cái xe máy is also fine.
Classifier + này: pointing at a thing.
Animals take con: never cái chó.
cái is the everyday classifier for things.
kia points at something farther away.
Number, then classifier, then noun: never ba cá.
The classifier goes first and này goes after the noun.
chiếc is the classifier for vehicles.
đôi for pairs: đôi giày is a pair of shoes.
tờ for flat sheets: paper, newspapers, banknotes.
bức for pictures and letters.
người is the classifier for people.
Also: Đây là cái gì?
kia goes after the noun, just like này.
Chicken pho: phở gà. The describing word comes after the noun.
In Vietnam, bánh mì means bread as well as the sandwich.
Word by word: coffee, milk, ice.
Weak iced tea, the everyday street-stall drink.
quá after an adjective: so, really.
A Hanoi lunch favorite.
Hanoi name. In the South: chả giò.
cơm (rice) comes first, then gà (chicken).
đen (black) comes after cà phê.
Number, then chai (bottle), then the drink.
nước is water.
sinh tố is a smoothie; the fruit comes after it.
bát is a bowl. To an older stall-holder, say Cho em instead.
Many cafés just say menu.
Literally: I don't eat spicy.
Literally: I eat vegetarian. chay and cay differ in the first sound.
Em ơi calls someone younger than you.
Literally: wishing you health.

meaning: Do you have a red shirt? (to a saleswoman)
note: có … không? = do you have …? màu đỏ comes after áo.

meaning: Can you take a little off?
note: Haggling in markets. Not in supermarkets.
Literally "long shirt": dài (long) comes after áo.
Point, and put cái này at the front.

meaning: How much for a kilo of mangoes?
note: cân is a kilo at the market.
quá goes after the adjective.
chỉ … thôi = only, just.
khác (other) comes after màu.

meaning: Do you have a bigger size?
note: hơn goes after the adjective: to hơn = bigger.
lấy = to take.
xanh covers both blue and green.
quần (pants) first, then the color.
thử after a verb: try doing it.
A counteroffer when you haggle.
đi chợ is also the everyday phrase for grocery shopping.
bằng = by, with.
Literally "second": the week counts from Sunday, chủ nhật.
thứ + a number. Days are lowercase in Vietnamese.
The one day with its own name, not a number.
rưỡi = and a half.
sáng (morning) comes after the hour.
tối (evening) comes after the hour.
sau (after) comes after tuần. Last week: tuần trước.
Month nine: tháng + a number, lowercase.
Day first, then month: ngày, then tháng.
thứ mấy asks for the day of the week.
You will also hear ngày mấy.
đang shows the action is going on now.

meaning: I went to Hoi An yesterday.
note: đã shows the action is done; with hôm qua you can leave it out.
sẽ = will. mai is short for ngày mai.
ở đâu (where) goes at the end.
On the right: bên phải.
phải also means "right" as in correct: Phải không? (Right?)
In the South: quẹo trái.
ngã tư: literally "four-way crossing".
rồi joins steps: and then.
Opposite: xa (far).
có … không around an adjective: is it …?

meaning: How far is Hoan Kiem Lake from here?
note: The place comes first; cách đây bao xa (how far from here) goes at the end.

meaning: How long does it take on foot?
note: đi bộ = walk; mất = it takes (time).

meaning: Is there a café near here?
note: có … không = is there …?

meaning: The hotel is next to the bank.
note: ở = is at, with no là. bên cạnh (next to) goes before the place, as in English.

meaning: The post office is across from the market.
note: đối diện = across from, facing.

meaning: Could you give me directions? (to a man a little older)
note: chỉ đường = show the way; giúp = for (me), as a favor.
bị: something bad that happens to you.
Literally "hug vehicle".
vé (ticket) first, then what kind.
To a driver.

meaning: Take me to Noi Bai Airport.
note: Cho tôi đến + place: what you say to a taxi or xe ôm driver.

meaning: Please slow down a little. (to a male driver)
note: nhé softens the request.
bằng = by (a vehicle), not với (with).

meaning: What time does the train leave?
note: chạy = run: trains and buses "run".
đi Huế: no word for "to" before the place.
One-way: vé một chiều.

meaning: How much is it to the airport?
note: hết = it comes to (a total).
Literally "I already booked a room."
bị for bad news; hoãn = postponed.
đây at the end: here it is.

meaning: Does this bus go to Hoan Kiem Lake?
note: này after the noun: xe buýt này (this bus).

A school student (up to grade 12): học sinh.
A college student: sinh viên.
The name comes after: công ty du lịch (travel company).
biết + verb: know how to.
A skill you learned usually takes biết.
không goes before biết.

meaning: Your Vietnamese is really good! (to a friend)
note: You will hear this a lot. A modest reply: Chưa giỏi đâu (Not really good yet).

meaning: How can I help you? (to a man)
note: có thể = can, be able to. Staff say this to customers.
đang: happening now, in this period.
đang: in the middle of it right now.
Noun first, then của + owner.

meaning: I go to work at eight.
note: lúc = at (a clock time).
bài tập = exercises; về nhà = (to take) home.

meaning: Excuse me, I have a question. (student to a female teacher)
note: Students call a female teacher cô and say em for "I".
Hanoi word. In the South, ốm means thin; sick is bệnh.

bị: for things that happen to you.
đau + body part: đau đầu (head), đau bụng (belly).

meaning: I need to see a doctor.
note: cần = need.
đi at the end: do it now.
gần nhất (nearest) comes after the noun.
Swap in your allergy: dị ứng tôm (shrimp), dị ứng lạc (peanuts).

meaning: Do you have cold medicine? (to a female pharmacist)
note: thuốc = medicine; cảm = a cold.

bị again: losing something is bad luck. Phone: điện thoại.

gì stays at the end, where the answer goes.
người (person) first, then the country: người Mỹ.

meaning: Where are you from? (to a friend)
note: Literally "You are a person of which country?"
đến từ = come from.
gốc Việt = of Vietnamese origin.

meaning: I was born in the US.
note: The verb stays the same: no "was" needed.
quê = home town, home province.
verb + được: able to.

meaning: I've been in Vietnam for three weeks.
note: được + time + rồi: for (so far).
No "have" and no là: Tôi + number + tuổi.

meaning: What do you do (for work)? (to a man a little older)
note: To a woman a little older: Chị làm nghề gì?
là joins two nouns: I = office worker.

Literally "I already have a family."
No là before đẹp: adjectives work like verbs.
Not the English word to.
adjective + hơn = more … than.
quá after the adjective: so, too.

meaning: The pho here is really good.
note: lắm after the adjective: very.
rất goes before the adjective.
cũ (old, used) comes after the noun. For people, old is già.

meaning: This room is a bit small.
note: hơi = a bit, before the adjective.
không + adjective, with no là.
adjective + bằng = as … as.
nhất (most) comes after the adjective, and both come after the noun.

meaning: This one is bigger than that one.

yên tĩnh (quiet) after the noun.

bao giờ means the same.

note: Answer Rồi or Chưa, not Không.

Answers a … chưa? question. Not Không.

Agreeing politely. In the South: dạ.

A polite no to someone older.

meaning: Thank you. (polite, to an older woman)

meaning: Please have a seat. (to a woman your parents' age)

note: xin phép = ask permission: the polite way to leave.

note: A guest (cháu) to a woman host. To a man: Chú nấu ăn ngon quá!

From older to younger, or between friends.
em to a man a little older. To a woman: Chị giỏi thật đấy!
Anyone.
Anyone, any good result.
em to a woman a little older. To a man: Anh làm nhanh thật!

An older person to em; hard work is a top virtue.
em to a woman a little older. To a man: Anh tốt bụng quá.
The usual "you're funny". To a woman: Chị vui tính quá!
To a friend your age.
Lovely in manner; to a woman a little older. To a man: Anh dễ thương quá!
Often heard at karaoke. To a man: Anh hát hay quá!

note: em to a woman a little older.
em to a woman a little older. To a man: …hợp với anh lắm.

Anyone; for a photo on a phone or on the wall.

note: What people tell the learner. To a woman: Chị nói…

Downplays your cooking or your work; the modest answer.

Lit. "I wouldn't dare". Polite and a little old-fashioned; to elders.
About a woman, girl or child; not said of men. Mild.
About a woman. Warmer than xinh.
Only about a man. Mild to warm.
Anyone, very common. Mild.
Anyone. Warm.
Mostly about a woman; a compliment people treasure. Warm.
Anyone. Warm, a little romantic.
Usually about a woman. Warm.
Anyone. Mild.

Anyone. Mild.
Anyone. Mild.
Anyone. Mild.
Anyone. Mild.
Anyone. Bold; fine for adults, not crude.

đôi mắt = (a pair of) eyes, softer and more poetic. Warm.

giọng nói = speaking voice; giọng Hà Nội = a Hanoi accent. Mild.
From French goût: đúng gu = just my type.

Standard word. Mild.
Young people, playful; online and in person.

meaning: You're so pretty! (he says to her)

meaning: You look really pretty today. (he says to her)
note: A woman to a man: Hôm nay anh đẹp trai lắm. Warm.

meaning: You look beautiful tonight. (he says to her)

note: A man to a woman: Em xinh quá! Warm.

meaning: You're really charming. (he says to her)

meaning: I love your smile. (he says to her)

meaning: You're so romantic! (she says to him)
note: A man to a woman: Em lãng mạn quá! Warm.

meaning: You're so gentle. (he says to her)

Sao vậy? = What's the matter? South uses vậy, Hanoi often thế.
Thế thôi. = That's all. Alone, Thôi! = Stop! / Enough!
Đẹp đấy! = That's nice! Hanoi; South: đó.
At the end: Cảm ơn chị ạ. Leave it out with friends.
After the name or kinship word: Anh ơi! Em ơi!
Mai gặp nhé. = See you tomorrow, OK? South: nha.
Đẹp nhỉ? = Pretty, isn't it? Also to oneself: Tên là gì nhỉ?
Anh đi à? = Oh, you're going? Checks what you think you just learned.
Được chứ! = Sure! Also checking: Anh đi chứ?
Em muốn cái này cơ! = I want THIS one!
Thế ư? = Is that so? Gentle, a bit literary.
Anh Minh kìa! = There's Minh!
Ăn cái đã! = Let's eat first!
